name: iced (iced-x86)
baseline: Capstone, Zydis and Intel XED (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries; objdump was not tested)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB code section of Firefox 86's 64-bit xul.dll, looped 20 times, measured in MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 256.69 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48, diStorm 92.17 MB/s. Decode plus format: 149.21 MB/s versus diStorm 58.85, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 10.6x Capstone, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Linux (Kubuntu 21.04), gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1. The C libraries are built by make-all.sh in the benchmark repo (CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, BeaEngine -O3 -flto); the Rust benchmark programs are built by their own per-library Makefiles, whose flags were not inspected.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (bindings for .NET, Java, Python, Lua, JavaScript via WebAssembly per its README); no C or C++ API in the repo, so C++ projects need FFI. Decoded instruction is 40 bytes and the decoder allocates nothing. Also contains an encoder and a code assembler.
caveats: The icedland/disas-bench repo is hosted by iced's own organisation (the original harness is athre0z's, per the MIT copyright line, 2017), so it is not a fully independent run; the published table is from June 2021 on a Skylake i5, with library versions of that date. The numbers are decode and decode+format throughput, not assembling speed, so GNU as, NASM and MASM are not the compared baselines. Capstone has no decode-only mode, so it appears only in the format table. Rust and C libraries use different formatters, so the decode+format column is not like for like in output text. A later fork by the yaxpeax author (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows iced decode at roughly 350 MB/s and yaxpeax-x86 about level with it (values read off the bars, so approximate).
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/assembler listed iced; WebSearch 'x86 disassembler benchmark Capstone Zydis XED' led to disas-bench

name: yaxpeax-x86
baseline: Capstone, Zydis and Intel XED (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB code section of Firefox 86's 64-bit xul.dll, looped 20 times, measured in MB/s.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 182.08 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48, udis86 80.72, diStorm 92.17 MB/s. Decode plus format: 40.05 MB/s versus Zydis 22.24, bddisasm 16.00, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02 MB/s, but behind iced (149.21) and diStorm (58.85). README: 'roughly 250mb/s decode throughput and on some hardware is the fastest software x86 decoder available'.
compiler_and_flags: Linux (Kubuntu 21.04), gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1. The C libraries are built by make-all.sh in the benchmark repo (CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, BeaEngine -O3 -flto); the Rust benchmark programs are built by their own per-library Makefiles, whose flags were not inspected.
tradeoffs: Rust crate in the yaxpeax decoder family; no C or C++ API, so C++ projects need FFI. Disassembler only (no assembler).
caveats: The table comes from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K, yaxpeax-x86 of that date); the yaxpeax author keeps a fork updated to yaxpeax-x86 2.0.0 (2024) whose result is only a bar chart. The README calls the in-repo benchmark 'so unrealistic as to be unuseful' and defers to disas-bench. Decode and decode+format throughput, not assembler speed; baselines are not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: README of github.com/iximeow/yaxpeax-x86 and disas-bench candidate list

name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86 and BeaEngine (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB code section of Firefox 86's 64-bit xul.dll, looped 20 times, measured in MB/s.
claimed_speedup: Decode plus format: 58.85 MB/s versus Zydis 22.24, bddisasm 16.00, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02, BeaEngine 13.42, udis86 12.02 MB/s (about 4.2x Capstone, derived from page data); second only to iced (149.21). Decode only: 92.17 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, bddisasm 35.48, Zydis 34.19, udis86 80.72 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Linux (Kubuntu 21.04), gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1. The C libraries are built by make-all.sh in the benchmark repo (CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, BeaEngine -O3 -flto); the Rust benchmark programs are built by their own per-library Makefiles, whose flags were not inspected.
tradeoffs: Plain C with a single API (about 45 KB per its README), callable directly from C++. Decodes x86/AMD64 only; coverage of recent instruction-set extensions was not checked.
caveats: The table is from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm of that date; the last commit on the default branch is December 2021, so newer instruction sets are probably missing. The README itself only quotes a 2014 thesis ('chose diStorm3, which had the best performance') and gives no numbers. Decode and decode+format throughput, not assembler speed; baselines are not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: disas-bench results table (second place in decode+format)

name: aron
baseline: macOS as (the system assembler on macOS, not GNU as)
workload: Assembling the repo's test.macos.s file (x86-64) with aron versus the macOS assembler.
claimed_speedup: 'aron is 12.94 ± 2.34 times faster than as' (text of the README benchmark image).
tradeoffs: Incomplete x86-64 assembler (README says so); outputs ELF and Mach-O objects; supports only part of the instruction set and directives, so it cannot replace GNU as, NASM or MASM on general input.
caveats: The README says 'This is not empirical by any means'. One input file, no command, hardware or flags stated, and the baseline is macOS as rather than GNU as. The language is inferred from Cargo.toml and rustfmt.toml because the repo page shows no language bar. The speedup probably reflects the narrower feature set.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'assembler faster than GNU as NASM benchmark assemble time github'

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 output (search starts from llvm -O0 binaries); also OpenSSL's expert hand-written assembly for one kernel
workload: Runtime of loop-free x86-64 kernels rewritten by a stochastic superoptimizer: Hacker's Delight bit tricks, the OpenSSL Montgomery multiplication kernel, SAXPY and a linked-list traversal.
claimed_speedup: Figure 1 of the ASPLOS 2013 paper: the Montgomery multiplication kernel from the OpenSSL big number library is 16 lines shorter, 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output, and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly. Abstract: STOKE produces programs that 'either match or outperform the code produced by gcc -O3, icc -O3, and in some cases, expert handwritten assembly'.
compiler_and_flags: Inputs compiled with llvm -O0; comparison code from gcc -O3 and icc -O3 (versions not stated in the text read). README example builds with g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline.
hardware: Search ran on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons with 30-minute budgets; the machine that timed the kernels was not identified in the text read. Current STOKE targets modern 64-bit x86 and runs best on Haswell or later.
tradeoffs: Superoptimizer that rewrites x86-64 assembly rather than an assembler; needs test cases, an SMT solver stack and many dependencies, and searches for tens of minutes per kernel. Targets x86-64 only and runs best on Haswell or later.
caveats: The paper is from 2013 and the speedups are on a small set of hand-picked loop-free kernels, measured relative to llvm -O0 starting points in Figure 11. The README admits 'We're not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'. The category fit (assembly tooling) is a judgement call; the baselines are compilers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: README of github.com/StanfordPL/stoke linking docs/papers/asplos13.pdf (fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: MaxAs
baseline: cuBLAS sgemm (NVIDIA's library kernels, compiled by NVIDIA's toolchain)
workload: Hand-scheduled single-precision GEMM kernels written in Maxwell SASS and assembled with MaxAs, versus cuBLAS sgemm, on large (4096) and small matrices.
claimed_speedup: SGEMM walkthrough: 'performing as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread version) and 'beating cublas by 4.8%' at size 4096 (256-thread version); about 98% of theoretical peak on GM107 and 96% on GM204. Absolute GFLOPS appear only in chart images.
hardware: NVIDIA GM204 (Maxwell) at a sustained 1607 MHz core clock and 8000 MHz memory; GM107 also mentioned. Card model and cuBLAS version are not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Assembler for NVIDIA Maxwell SASS only (GTX 9xx era), written in Perl; the repository is archived and Intel has discontinued the project. Gains come from hand-written kernels and scheduling, not from the assembler alone.
caveats: First-party wiki claim; exact per-size GFLOPS are only in images, and the page names no cuBLAS version, CUDA version or flags. The speedup is of a hand-written kernel against a 2015-era library, not of the assembler against GNU as, NASM or MASM. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.
found_via: GitHub: README and SGEMM wiki page of NervanaSystems/maxas, found while looking for GPU (SASS) assemblers

name: Fadec
baseline: libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis (x86 decoding libraries)
workload: Decoding x86-32 and x86-64 instructions with a lookup-table decoder; a separate x86-64 encoder is included.
claimed_speedup: 'Fadec is significantly faster than libopcodes, Capstone, or Zydis due to the absence of high-level abstractions and the small lookup table' (no numbers); encoder API v2 'about 3x faster than v1' (internal comparison).
stars_or_usage: 235 stars; search results also showed a copy under Android's external/lfi tree and an oleavr/fadec fork (neither opened)
tradeoffs: C library with no dependencies, about 95 KiB with decoder and encoder, usable in freestanding environments. Targets Intel 64 behaviour; AMD-specific differences are not handled. Decoded operand sizes are not always exact for speed.
caveats: No benchmark numbers or harness in the repo (only a decode-profile.c program), and Fadec is absent from the public disas-bench candidate list. Tier D with notability argued from reuse rather than stars. Baselines are disassemblers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM.
found_via: GitHub: README text of github.com/aengelke/fadec; WebSearch 'fadec x86 decoder benchmark' showed no independent numbers
